MARC Raises $5 Million in Seed Funding Led by Work-Bench and MXV Capital.

New York-based proptech startup MARC has raised $5 million in seed funding, bringing its total funding to $6 million.

The round was led by Work-Bench and MXV Capital, with participation from Des Traynor, Mark Ghermezian, Ian Nolan, Cyrus Claffey, Daniel Eberhard and Brian Moran.

Led by founder and CEO Aaron Devitt, MARC develops an AI-powered spend intelligence platform for institutional real estate owners and operators.

The platform analyzes vendor contracts, validates invoices against agreed terms, tracks renewals and helps identify operating expense discrepancies across real estate portfolios.

According to the company, MARC manages more than $100 million in annual vendor spending across 30 US states and Canada.

The funding will support hiring across product, engineering and go-to-market functions, alongside expansion across North America.

“Joshi, if I join BookMyCA, what’s the guarantee I’ll get work?”

Chartered Accountants (CAs), Company Secretaries (CSs) and lawyers ask me this often. I can make an introduction. Whether it turns into work depends on what the client needs and whether both sides want to work together.

Five years ago, some of my clients could run their business by selling or exporting just one or two products. Today, those same clients need around 20 products just to stay in business.

I believe our profession is facing the same pressure in the AI era. Small firms need to offer more services to keep going. That’s what I mean by generalisation.

A client may come to me for GST filing. Later, the same client may need a CA for an income tax matter, a CS for company filings with the ROC, or a lawyer to check a contract. Hiring someone full-time for every kind of work gets expensive. A small firm can help that client with more by working with people it trusts.

Even before BookMyCA, professionals would call me to discuss a case or share an opportunity. A few of those calls led to work. Over time, those conversations also helped me learn who I could call for different kinds of work.

That’s why I started BookMyCA. I want business owners in India to find the right help. I also want CAs, CSs and lawyers to get to know each other before a client needs them.

When I introduce someone to a client, my client is trusting my judgement too. I want to know two simple things. Have they handled this kind of work before? Will they call back when they say they will?

This profession has given me a lot. BookMyCA is one way I want to give back. If people remember me as someone who saw a problem in his own work and gave it an honest try, I’d be happy with that.

They treat it like outsourcing: hand over a spec, hope for the best.
That's not how it works when it works.

Here's what actually makes it succeed:
1. The engineers join YOUR standups, YOUR Slack, YOUR sprint board.
Not a separate team. Your team, just bigger.
2. You start with one role, not five.
Prove the fit in 2 to 4 weeks, then scale.
3. You pick the model that fits the work.
Monthly for ongoing roadmap work.
Contract for a fixed stretch.
Per project when the scope is clear.
4. You keep ownership.
Code, repos, decisions. All yours from day one.
5. You plan the exit before the start.

Good augmentation leaves documentation, not dependency.

The goal was never to replace your team.
It's to stop your roadmap waiting on your hiring pipeline.

BLS indicates 2 million out of work for more than 6 months, similar to previous downturns, except… we’re not IN a recession. And the impact of this war and an unprecedented energy crisis could push us into one. Then what?

Companies aren’t simply eliminating positions. They’re eliminating layers of specialization, redistributing responsibilities, and expecting remaining employees to absorb the work.

UI/UX is a perfect but not one off example.

Nielsen Norman Group’s State of UX 2026 report identified companies compressing responsibilities previously handled by several specialists into individual positions, creating leaner teams with greater demands. And this is typical of many fields impacted by RIFs over the past 4 years.

What happens if companies are forced to freeze hiring or lay more people off while already running lean?

This goes far beyond COVID overhiring. This is restructuring of epic proportions, with enormous risk.

And it creates two problems simultaneously.

Experienced designers who previously commanded $180,000–$250,000 compete for fewer specialist positions. Those who land are now responsible for the work of several people. It’s not increased productivity. It’s working harder and longer to meet deadlines, potentially sacrificing quality and sustainability.

Indeed Hiring Lab’s June 2026 analysis found job postings in software development, marketing, and data analysis roughly 30% or more below February 2020 levels.

The 2025 State of User Research report found 26% of respondents reported layoffs affecting product/UX design departments and 21% in product management.

Traditionally, recovery means companies start hiring again. But with this restructuring, if an employer previously needed 8 people to support a function and now operates with 3, recovery doesn’t necessarily restore the other 5 positions.

Doesn’t the recession risk become especially serious? A company already operating with minimum staffing has fewer nonessential roles left to cut. If revenues contract, it may have to cut the people actually keeping operations functioning. Would they simply stop laying people off because they’re already running so lean? That seems unlikely.

Are companies replacing design teams with one exceptionally versatile person? Or accepting less work, lower quality, and assuming that if one team fails, they can replace it with people more desperate to work? These are different business decisions, but it all means fewer jobs and higher expectations of workers. And AI hasn’t shown it can fill gaps this large, yet.

I don’t know the answer. I’m an avid researcher, not an economist, but the data is not as simple as the headline BLS number. It doesn’t capture every variation of job loss, underemployment, people pushed out of the workforce who are struggling, or those still technically employed while searching for their next job.

𝗗𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝘀𝘁𝘀 𝗔𝗿𝗲𝗻'𝘁 𝗨𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿-𝗧𝗼𝗼𝗹𝗲𝗱. 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘆'𝗿𝗲 𝗢𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗼𝗹𝗱. 

Count the pitches a practice owner gets in a week. AI that reads X-rays. AI that answers phones. AI that verifies insurance. A new PMS. A reviews tool. A financing partner. An agency promising 40 new patients a month.

𝗘𝗮𝗰𝗵 𝘀𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗲𝘀 𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺. 𝗧𝗼𝗴𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿, 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗮 𝗻𝗲𝘄 𝗼𝗻𝗲.

I have advised 100’s of practice owners. The most common pattern wasn't doctors lacking tools. It was being buried in them: software half the team never opened, a new agency every 18 months, and a constant feeling of being behind.

𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁'𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗮 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗳𝗹𝗮𝘄. 𝗜𝘁'𝘀 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗰𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗯𝘂𝘆𝗲𝗿 𝗯𝗲𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗶𝗼𝗿.

There are more than 250 dental practice management products alone. In the ADA Health Policy Institute's mid-2026 survey, 43% of dentists already use AI for at least one task, and another 26% plan to.

Meanwhile, the buyer is stretched:
𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗶𝗻𝘀: Dentists' inflation-adjusted income was flat in 2025, extending a 15-year decline. Over five years, revenue grew 1.4% while expenses rose 4.9%.
 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗴: The #1 challenge for 2026 (54%), followed by overhead (42%).
𝗧𝗶𝗺𝗲: About a third of dentists say they're overworked.
A squeezed, short-staffed, tired owner is exactly the buyer most vulnerable to "this tool will fix it."

What the research says happens to buyers…

In the classic jam study, shoppers who saw 6 options were about 10x more likely to buy than those who saw 24. Replications are mixed, but a 2015 meta-analysis (Chernev et al., ~7,200 people) shows when overload reliably hits: the decision is hard, the options are complex, the buyer is unsure what they want, and they're short on time and energy. 

That's a dentist comparing AI imaging, a new PMS and a phone platform between patients. The results: lower confidence, more regret, delayed decisions and more switching.

Overwhelm leads to regret. CEB found purchases took 97% longer than buyers expected, and the more overwhelming the purchase, the more likely buyers regretted it.

What it looks like in a practice:
• The Frankenstack: seven tools, seven logins, seven contracts, and "integration coming soon."
• Shelfware: bought after a great demo, never implemented because nobody owns it.
• The owner as IT director: managing vendors and renewals on top of producing.
• Symptom shopping: buying software for a leadership, hiring or case-acceptance problem.

A tool amplifies a system. It doesn't replace one.

𝗔 𝗳𝗶𝗹𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗻𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗱𝗲𝗺𝗼
1. What's the constraint? Name the one number you're trying to move.
2. Who owns it? No one with time to implement it? Don't buy yet.
3. What does it replace? Subtract before you add.
4. What's the 90-day proof? Get a measurable outcome in writing.
5. When's your stack audit? Once a year, cancel what nobody uses.
6. Who's your prescriber? Find one advisor with nothing to sell who'll say, "Don't buy that."

2. How to organize. How to separate signal from noise. How to recover quickly from being knocked down. (Behavioral)

- thinking on your feet under pressure
 
- structuring your career

-handling pressure, stress and anxiety 

We’re going to launch seminars to help in these areas — the trifecta of needs for lack of a better word. An MDR contract pays for a team of analysts. AI is supposed to change that arithmetic, but you won’t see any savings soon.

Rapid7’s CEO said the company’s goal is to deliver SOC results “with software-like leverage.” That means Rapid7 wants to be able to add customers without hiring more analysts for each one.

Currently, Rapid7 keeps about 72 cents of each dollar. The CFO said gross margin will shrink in the fourth quarter and beyond as AWS and AI charges ramp.

The AI costs start the day a feature goes into production. The savings depend on the software matching what analysts do today and on the company then deciding it needs fewer of them. Only the costs are certain.

Rapid7’s latest quarterly report also says it is cutting about 12 percent of its workforce. It doesn’t say how many of those roles are analysts, so a customer can’t tell from the filing whether the base service has the same people behind it.

At renewal, ask what the base service includes after the cut. If savings arrive, ask where they came from. And get response times and analyst access written into the contract.

I spent this year trying to answer one question properly: what is artificial intelligence actually doing to work?

Not "what could it do". Not "what are people afraid it will do". What the data shows, four years in.

Here is the whole portfolio. The complete edition, 118 pages, is linked in the first comment.

Exposure Is Not Adoption (paper, 129 months of BLS data). The U.S. information sector peaked in November 2022, the month ChatGPT shipped, and is now 12.1% below that peak. But twelve-month hiring growth peaked in August 2021, fifteen months earlier. The break is real. The attribution is not.

Hires Before Headcount (paper, JOLTS flows). The sector lost 381,000 jobs in 47 months without a layoff wave. Hires fell 33%; layoffs stayed far below their pandemic peak; quits fell 23%. It stopped replacing the people who left.

The Disclosure Gap (paper, 643 SEC filings). AI language in 10-Ks went from 38% of firms to 95% in four years. Within firms, more AI language predicts 1.25 points faster headcount growth and slower revenue per employee. That is what investment looks like, not substitution.

Measure the Door (policy brief). Five statistics and a six-question survey module that would settle the question, with the refutation conditions stated in advance.

AI × labour chart pack (workbook + dashboard). 129 months, four sectors, every number recomputed by a script in the repo.

ASC 606 workpaper (sample). What an audit trail for AI-assisted revenue recognition should look like: 16 risks, 14 controls, 25 contracts, zero errors reaching the ledger.

The Industry Mix Channel (paper, 51 states). A shift-share design on 2019 industry composition and published AI exposure scores. Flat pre-trends, a clean placebo, and a permutation p-value of 0.27. A null, with the diagnostics to trust it.

ensemble (tool + 25,968-word paper + live demo). Four models answer one prompt; one model cross-examines another. The demo is the run where half the providers failed and the report shipped anyway.

The AI jobs number nobody is watching (essay, 2 pages). The same argument for a general reader: 381,000 jobs lost without a layoff wave, and the entry-level statistic that would catch it.

Every artifact is open, every number is reproducible from a script, and none of them claims more than the data supports. All eight are on one page: https://lnkd.in/dXimrCKf

Hiring internationally is the easy part. Letting someone go is where many companies get into trouble.

In the US, many founders are used to "at-will" employment. You can end a working relationship fairly quickly.

In many other countries, it works very differently:

→ You may need a valid, documented reason to end employment
→ Notice periods can be weeks or even months
→ Severance pay may be required by law
→ Some countries have extra protections for certain employees

A founder who ends an international employee's contract "the US way" can face legal claims, penalties, and damage to their reputation as an employer.

The fix is simple: understand the exit rules before you hire, not when you need them.

This is one area where an Employer of Record (EOR) really helps. Because the EOR is the legal employer in that country, they know the local rules and guide you through the process properly.

Deel offers EOR in 120+ countries, so you don't need to become an expert in every country's labor law.

Companies are treating layoffs like AI experiments.

Cut the team. Test AI. If it doesn't work, rehire.

Over the past year, a pattern has emerged that we call the reversible layoff. A company announces a workforce reduction and credits artificial intelligence, organizational restructuring, or efficiency improvements. A few months later, it quietly starts hiring again for many of the same roles.

Here is one such interesting report. Careerminds published a survey in February 2026. According to the survey, a sample of 600 HR leaders found that about a third of companies with AI-led layoffs had already rehired 25–50% of those roles. Most rehires happened within six months. Only 8.4% said the restructuring delivered what was promised.

This is the most logical boardroom line of thinking. For decision-making purposes, some companies think people are the most reversible cost.

Data centers, software contracts, and chips are long-term/ multi years commitments for all organizations. But people are not. The organization can save money by cutting 20–30% of a function if AI handles the work. In the worst case, if an AI experiment falls short, they can rehire experienced candidates from resource pools. The downside of workforce restructuring is limited for the company, but it can have a severe financial and emotional impact on the worker.

Even if the same organization starts hiring again, things would be different. Rehire roles are often lower-paying, contract, or outsourced.

The company can push the undo button. Your career doesn't.

We call this the Reversible Layoff.

Working professionals should watch closely. You can't control your employer's experiments, but you can prevent or reorient to reduce the impact.  

These are the three questions to ask yourself this week:

Is my work most adaptable for AI to test? - High-volume, rules-based, easy to measure: customer support, first-draft content, routine analysis, QA.
Am I one of the few resources within the organization who knows why things break? - Institutional knowledge was the most-cited loss in the rehiring data. Make yours visible.
Do I have a financial reserve if my department can be tested for AI adoption or implementation? - A six-month expense outlook and a financial reserve to withstand sudden changes can turn a reversible layoff from a crisis into a decision.

Then there are clients who want AI in everything. I like the energy, but I always slow it down.
 
Fast adoption goes wrong the same way every time. The output sounds so confident that people stop checking it. Then it gets something wrong, and nobody trusts it again. So I pick one job first, run it for a couple of weeks, and see if it actually saves time before touching anything else.
 
First I ask whether a rule can do it. If the input is a form field, a number, a date or a known keyword, rules do it better. They’re cheaper, they’re exact, and you can see why they did what they did. I only bring in AI when the input is messy, and the meaning has to be understood.
 
That looks like this:
- Summarising a long email thread or document so someone can catch up in a minute
- Drafting a first reply in the right tone, which a person reads and edits
- Reading scanned or photographed documents and invoices and turning them into data
- Working out what an email is asking for when it doesn’t follow any pattern
- Searching your files by meaning, like “the contract where we agreed the late fee”
- Pulling details out of free text where the layout is different every time
 
Where it struggles: exact facts like figures, dates and references, unusual cases it hasn’t seen, and decisions that need someone responsible, because a model can’t be.
 
So I put AI on top of rules, not instead of them. The rules do the parts that must be exact, like deadlines, invoices and approvals. The AI handles the messy reading and drafting. A person checks anything that matters before it goes out.
A generic chatbot also doesn’t know your business. A custom setup uses your own records and your rules, but it costs more, and the cost doesn’t stop at the build. There are usage fees, monitoring and fixes.
 
The upside is real: time saved on repetitive work, and more capacity without hiring at the same pace. The downside is output that needs checking, running costs, and people trusting it too much.
AI speeds up a process that already works. If your process is a mess, you just get the mess faster.

🚀 API Testing – What Should a Manual Tester Validate?
Many testers think API testing is just sending a request and checking whether the status code is 200 OK.


But API testing goes beyond that!
As a Manual Tester, here are the important validations I always consider:
✅ Status Code – Is the API returning the correct status code?
✅ Response Body – Are all expected fields present?
✅ Data Accuracy – Are the returned values correct?
✅ Headers – Are the required headers available?
✅ Schema Validation – Are the field names and data types correct?
✅ Error Handling – Does the API handle invalid inputs properly?
✅ Response Time – Does the API meet performance expectations?
✅ Authentication & Authorization – Can only authorized users access the data?
✅ Boundary Testing – What happens with null, empty, minimum and maximum values?

💡 Real-time example:
API: GET /users/123
Expected validations:
Status code: 200 OK
User ID should be 123
Name and email should be returned correctly
Response structure should match the API contract
Response time should meet the agreed SLA

If the user doesn't exist, the API should return the expected error response, such as 404 Not Found.

Remember: A 200 OK response doesn't always mean the API is working correctly!
Test the response, validate the data, and verify the business logic.
Happy Testing! 💻

Spent this morning with Matt Knowles from NorthStar People and we kept coming back to the same thing. The hardest roles I’m trying to fill in MedTech AI right now aren’t really roles at all, they’re combinations.

There are plenty of good ML engineers and plenty of good regulatory people. What there isn’t is enough people who are properly both.

Day to day, the profiles everyone wants and almost nobody can find look something like this:

AI regulatory affairs: Someone who knows MDR and IVDR inside out and can now hold their own on the EU AI Act, model validation and algorithm change control without treating them as separate jobs.
SaMD engineers: Software people who build to IEC 62304 and understand that a model that looks brilliant on a benchmark still has to survive a technical file.
Clinical AI: Clinicians with real ML literacy, or engineers who’ve spent years inside clinical product teams and can tell you whether it actually works on a ward and own clinical safety when it goes live.
MLOps, regulated: Anyone can deploy a model; deploying one you can trace, document and monitor for drift with a notified body watching is different.
AI and cyber in one head: Securing clinical systems and governing AI risk at the same time — most org charts haven’t got a title for it yet.

Plenty of candidates have two of those boxes ticked, a few have three, and the ones with everything are being chased by MedTech, big tech and well-funded scale-ups.

That’s why this can’t be done off a keyword search and a pile of CVs. You have to spot who’s 70% there and know which 30% can be built around them. Sometimes the answer is two people who cover each other’s gaps, or a contract specialist bridging the AI Act piece while the team grows into it.

So, I’m genuinely curious: whether you’re hiring in MedTech or you’re one of these rare people yourself, which profile is the hardest to find right now, and is it a real shortage, or is the industry just asking for unicorns?

Frasca Executive Dispatch | Wednesday: AI (Enterprise / Leadership)

The AI budget has quietly become a labor budget. I have built AI companies since the 1990s. In every wave, the technology arrived first and the cost discipline arrived late. Three items this week put the cost question on the CFO's desk.

1. On 10 November, OpenAI's Greg Brockman announced that JPMorganChase signed a contract to use Codex agents to write, review, debug and ship code, per American Banker. CFO Jeremy Barnum said last month the bank spends "something like $700 million annually" on AI, and cited token costs as an offset to the benefits.

2. Also on 10 November, Reuters reported McKinsey's Global Banking Annual Review: token spending for AI agents "could easily reach 20% of total labor costs." Senior partner Vik Sohoni said routing staff to cheaper models stops working once agents talk to each other.

3. On 9 November, Fortune reported an SHL survey: 19.1% of US respondents said they were replaced by AI and later asked back. A separate Robert Half survey found 32% of US hiring managers who cut roles because of AI later reinstated them. Of those, 40% cited institutional knowledge AI could not replace.

What this rhymes with: early cloud. The bills arrived before the operating model did.

Second-order effect: agents are now a variable labor cost with no headcount line. Firms that cut people first can end up paying twice, once in tokens and once to rehire.

For institutions: budget agents like headcount. Name an owner, a unit cost and a reversal plan before a role is removed.

AI doesn't replace experience. It compresses it.

— Rob Frasca | COSIMO Digital | cosimodigital.com
Capital markets, rebuilt on-chain, amplified by AI

“Skills over headcount” is the polite way of saying “we’d rather not train anyone anymore.”

India’s GCCs are one of the country’s biggest talent success stories. And rightly so.

But look at who they are hiring now.

foundit’s data shows the entry-level share of GCC hiring has dropped from 42% to 30%. Professionals with four to six years of experience have gone from 26% to 34%. And GCCs are reportedly offering up to a 40% salary premium for AI talent (Storyboard18).

So the pay is going up, and the door is getting narrower.

Business Today reports they are also hiring fewer full-timers and more AI contractors, breaking one broad role into specific skills brought in as needed.

On paper, this is smart. Lean teams, precise skills, faster output.

But here’s where it gets interesting.

What does a 22-year-old hear? Be skilled before anyone gives you the chance to learn.

If the entry-level role keeps shrinking, how does anyone become a senior hire? If every role is a rented skill, who holds the knowledge when the contract ends?

Companies call it capability. A fresher calls it a locked door.

Every organisation wants senior talent. Very few want to be the place that builds it.

I actually think this is one of the more uncomfortable questions in talent strategy right now. The answer isn’t to go back to mass hiring. It’s to be honest about who pays for learning when nobody wants to.

Curious how founders, CEOs and talent leaders see this.

Is skills-first hiring the smartest shift in years, or a way of outsourcing the cost of learning to everyone else?

Executive search sounds expensive, and terms differ from firm to firm.
But for hard roles it pays off: when the right person barely exists on the market, and the few who do aren't job hunting or replying to postings, standard recruiting simply doesn't work.

What does that look like in practice?

A startup called 42 came to us. They build autonomous AI agents for HFT research, and needed an architect to design an agent system covering the full research cycle: from generating hypotheses to testing and launch. There's no ready-made playbook for a role like this, and people with real experience building autonomous research agents are rare.

What worked wasn't a flood of applications, but an accumulated pipeline: we'd already run searches for this client, and our recruiter Valeriya Soboleva reviewed those profiles against the new role. One candidate had built a co-scientist system for processing hypotheses and had trading experience. A couple of interviews with the CPO and founder, and an offer.

📎 Read the full case here: https://lnkd.in/eUW5i85B

That's the essence of retained search: we start not from the vacancy but from the market, we see its boundaries and understand what's realistically possible on role, timeline and compensation before the search even begins. Our value isn't access to candidates, it's knowing what will actually work in a specific context.

But an expensive model doesn't guarantee the result on its own: payment structure, guarantees, interview speed and handling counteroffers matter as much as the search itself. A lot here depends on both sides, so we work as partners: we align on expectations, keep the process transparent and get to the offer together.

How this process works step by step, when retained search truly pays off, and what to check in the contract, we broke it all down in the article. Link in the comments 👇

California's school districts are changing superintendents at a pace that should worry every board member, and the numbers now confirm it is not a blip.

In the 2024-25 school year, 18.9 percent of California school districts changed superintendents, up from 11.8 percent before the pandemic. Nationally the rate reached 17.1 percent. In Sonoma County, nearly one in four districts, 9 of 38, turned over their chief this year. A study of the country's 500 largest districts found 23 percent had at least one leadership change in 2024-25. Researchers at The Superintendent Lab now call leadership churn the new normal.

Los Angeles Unified is the sharpest example of what churn costs. Alberto Carvalho resigned in June amid an FBI investigation tied to a 6.2 million dollar AI chatbot contract, after being placed on paid administrative leave in February. Acting Superintendent Andres Chait leads the nation's second largest district while the board has set no timeline for a permanent replacement, and the district is losing two academic chiefs at the same time. It also faces budget deficits and declining enrollment.

The research is blunt about the damage. USC professor Julie Marsh notes that when turnover hits, a new leader may shift priorities or stop reforms, which lowers staff morale and disrupts programs and policies. Continuity is not a luxury in a district. It is the condition that lets a multi-year improvement plan survive long enough to work.

Some boards are responding with a different hiring instinct. West Contra Costa Unified turned to Cheryl Cotton, a homegrown leader who grew up in the district and served five years as a deputy superintendent at the state Department of Education. She arrived with a 100-day plan, "Building a Stronger WCCUSD," that names the district's real problems, declining enrollment, budget deficits, and inconsistent academic outcomes, in plain language. Boards are increasingly betting that a leader who already knows the community can hold the line where an outsider would need a year to learn it.

The leadership lesson here is about systems, not personalities. A board that treats the superintendency as a single hire will keep reliving the same crisis. A board that builds a pipeline, documents its priorities, and keeps reforms alive through a transition is doing the work that actually protects students from churn.

If your district has lived through a leadership change in the last two years, what held steady, and what fell apart first?

“Our people are our greatest asset.”

If Australian customers help build your profits, Australian workers deserve investment too.
